articles.title: AI models can be tricked into identifying civilians as military targets by telling them it’s a game
articles.body:
Some AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and other leading AI labs could be easily tricked into identifying targets for military strikes — even if they include civilians or locations like schools — simply by being told they’re playing a game, according to a new research report by Vals.
Vals, a San Francisco-based AI evaluation startup, tested whether leading AI models could be manipulated into participating in autonomous warfare. Researchers used simulated scenarios and a combination of generated and real imagery from Ukraine and Iran to see if the AI models would mark targets in drone and satellite imagery.
The models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, and other companies frequently identified potential targets in drone and satellite imagery, including civilians and surrendering soldiers. When the models refused to cooperate, researchers were able to jailbreak them by claiming the battlefield scenarios were part of a game.
The findings come amid growing fears about the immediate risks posed by AI, beyond the existential threats associated with artificial general intelligence.
Earlier this year, Anthropic became embroiled in a dispute with the Department of Defense after it told the agency it could not use Anthropic’s technology for mass surveillance of Americans or autonomous warfare. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has insisted that today’s AI systems aren’t reliable enough to make life-or-death decisions without a human in the loop. Meanwhile, the Pentagon argued it should be able to deploy the technology for any lawful military purpose.
The new research raises further questions about whether AI companies are capable of preventing their models from being used in warfare.
Ironically, AI models from Anthropic performed the worst in these simulated scenarios. But none of the models performed particularly well. None of the researchers’ requests were blocked by a safety classifier, and refusals were uncommon. Even when models did refuse, they often complied after being told they were playing a game.
Anthropic spokesperson Eduardo Maia Silva told TechCrunch the company appreciates Vals’ report, recommendations, and collaboration, and acknowledged that the outcomes were not acceptable.
“The examples in the report are very clearly against our rules and we have banned and will ban users when we see this behavior,” according to an emailed company statement sent by Silva. “Even for authorized settings, Anthropic has long been firm that today’s frontier AI systems are not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.”
Anthropic told TechCrunch that its teams were already developing additional safeguards before the report was published and that those measures would be in place soon. Anthropic is also expanding its own testing and enhancing safeguards and enforcement to address any gaps it finds.
OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans told TechCrunch the company prohibits using its public models to facilitate violence or for unapproved national security purposes, including in the scenarios Vals simulated.
“We actively detect and disrupt misuse, including by suspending accounts that violate our policies,” OpenAI said in an emailed statement. “We’re also developing additional safeguards for our public models against misuse involving drones and drone software.”
Vals notes in the report that the models were never asked to directly make strike decisions, a task the researchers said the models would typically refuse. That doesn’t mean their outputs couldn’t have dire or fatal consequences in the real world. For instance, targeting information could be used by autonomous weapons systems.
In some scenarios, the models were asked to report whether people were visible. Positive reports were followed by simulated strikes and the models would see the consequences.
The report relies on commercial models from frontier AI labs, not the models those companies might provide to the military. It’s not clear whether the additional safeguards would apply to military use, though.
Vals also noted that technical challenges, including latency and limited onboard computing capacity, make it difficult to use general-purpose AI models for live drone targeting. Those constraints make their deployment in combat less of an immediate threat.
A more immediate threat, the researchers say, is that AI models could be used to annotate battlefield footage at scale, producing training data for autonomous targeting systems.
For instance, researchers relied on real satellite imagery of an Iranian school that was bombed by the U.S. in February 2026, killing more than 150 civilians. Bloomberg later reported that an “overreliance on AI” contributed to the strike. In Vals’ testing, models frequently marked the school, which sat next to a military complex, as a strike target, with Claude Opus 5.5 selecting the school in 69% of ordinary trials and 72% of game-framed trials.
Anthropic no longer has an active Pentagon contract, but other companies, including SpaceXAI, OpenAI, and Google do. A recent Congressional Research Service report found that the Pentagon is not known to be using any frontier AI model in autonomous weapons systems directly.
TechCrunch has also reached out to Meta, Google, Thinking Machines Lab, and SpaceXAI for comment.

articles.title: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
articles.body:
The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The NSA closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to restore the network, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter.
The move to further restrict staffing levels came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. It is not clear what prompted the reversal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue.
The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said.
“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”
A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month.
“The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.”
The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. AI tools helped researchers exploit them, setting off a scramble by government agencies and corporations around the world to address the issue in recent weeks. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches.
The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords.
Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack.
A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One.
Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. “It could impact analysis and reporting, but for highest priority requirements they would find a way to work those. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.”
A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a system of three main levels that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail.
Sometime Tuesday evening, the inbox reverted to “code green,” instructing employees to report to work as scheduled. It was not immediately clear whether the outage was resolved. But later Tuesday night, the inbox moved to a “code orange,” closing the campus for most employees until further notice, according to the inbox recording and source familiar with the matter.
The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country.
All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas.
Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings.
And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts.
There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security.
The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official.
Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time.
This story has been updated with additional information.
Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting.
CNN’s Kylie Atwood and Haley Britzky contributed reporting.

articles.title: Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit
articles.body:
Physics > Physics and Society
  [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026]
Title:Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:More than 13,000 satellites operate in low Earth orbit (LEO), and concern has grown that nuclear weapons could be used in space to target them. Beyond the initial X-ray burst, electrons released by radioactive fission products can become trapped in Earth's magnetic field, repeatedly exposing satellites as an artificial radiation belt. Here we couple prompt radiation, electron trapping and belt evolution to satellite failures, collisions and atmospheric drag. For a 1-Mt detonation at 500km over the South Atlantic, repeated belt exposure disables approximately 98% of modeled satellites within one week in our central case. Tripling the assumed radiation tolerance delays widespread failure by only days: approximately 97% are still disabled within two weeks. The loss of maneuverability sharply increases collision risk, with approximately 20 collisions expected within two years. Drag removes many disabled spacecraft from lower altitudes, but replacement satellites could remain exposed to radiation and debris for years. These findings show how a single detonation could devastate orbital infrastructure and support efforts to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.

articles.title: Anthropic Paid Rubio's Ex-Chief of Staff's Firm $740k.it Lobbied His NSC
articles.body:
Anthropic Paid Rubio's Ex-Chief Of Staff's Firm $740,000. After The Jensen Memo, It Lobbied His NSC
In the months after Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote the memo that set off Jensen Huang's fall, Anthropic's two Trump-connected lobbying firms were working the offices Rubio runs, federal disclosures show. One is run in Washington by Rubio's former Senate chief of staff and counts Susie Wiles' daughter as a partner. The other is Wiles' old firm. Anthropic has paid the two $1.63 million since April 2025.
The first is Continental Strategy, which Anthropic has paid $740,000 since April 2025. Its Washington managing partner, Alberto Martinez, is named on all six of Continental's quarterly reports for the AI lab. Meanwhile, Continental's report for April through June lists the National Security Council (NSC) among the offices it lobbied, and its report for July through September lists the State Department. Rubio is both national security adviser and secretary of state.
Anthropic hired Ballard Partners on March 9, four days after the Pentagon labeled the company a supply-chain risk, Bloomberg reported. Wiles was a managing partner there until 2019. Ballard's first report, covering the rest of March, lists the White House Office and the Executive Office of the President. Ballard's report for April through June adds the NSC as well, and Anthropic has paid the firm $890,000 this year.
Rubio's memo, dated March 30, went to a handful of Cabinet secretaries ahead of Trump's May trip to China, according to the New York Times. Rubio wrote it from a CIA report, recasting the agency's findings "in his own more assertive terms," the Washington Post reported Friday, though CIA officials aren't convinced Alice Huang - the Chinese national at the center of Jensen Huang's ouster - knowingly passed anything to Beijing.
Huang tried at least three times to get a meeting with Rubio and never got one, two people familiar with the matter told the Washington Sun. Rubio's aides nixed proposed talks in the spring of 2025, again that summer and again early this year, with his office saying he was booked or couldn't accommodate the Nvidia chief. The snubs deepened fears inside Nvidia that powerful forces in the US government were out to undermine Huang's influence as a leading voice for closer economic ties with Beijing, the Sun reported.
Huang was Washington's loudest corporate backer of open-weight models, the cheap alternative to the closed systems Anthropic sells, and his exit clears the way for a crackdown on them. David Sacks argued on All-In that the ouster served Anthropic's "safetyist" allies, and physicist Steve Hsu wrote that he had heard Nvidia was planning "to go hard at producing frontier class open models" so it wouldn't depend on OpenAI or Anthropic.
In the past months I heard on very good authority that Jensen and Nvidia were planning to go hard at producing frontier class open models. 
They wanted to verticalize their AI presence, and not depend on OAI or ANT to drive the industry forward.
OAI, ANT, and GOOG are...
— steve hsu (@hsu_steve) November 12, 2026
Huang's ouster could be the best break Anthropic gets as it heads into its IPO this week. Under Huang, Nvidia built its own family of open models, Nemotron, backed startups including Reflection AI, Thinking Machines Lab and Poolside, and was moving to acquire Hugging Face. "Nvidia was on a titanic collision course with the labs," the CEO of a leading AI startup told Business Insider, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad called the ouster an attack on open models at a conference Monday.
Meanwhile, Trump said Monday he doesn't know that Alice Huang was a spy "at all," and defended Lutnick. He called Huang a "legend" after the resignation, and Huang was reportedly weighing a comeback as his Silicon Valley allies lean on Nvidia's board - which isn't considering it, the FT reported.
The Wiles Connection
By the third quarter Ballard's brief had widened from Pentagon procurement to "US policy regarding AI," and its report adds the Pentagon and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, with the NSC still on the list.
Two of the five Ballard lobbyists on that report came straight out of the national security apparatus. Amaryllis Fox Kennedy is listed as a CIA clandestine service officer from 2003 to 2009 and a deputy director of national intelligence in 2025 and 2026. Micah Ketchel, on the account since March, is listed as Rep. Mike Waltz's chief of staff from 2019 to 2025, then a senior adviser to the national security adviser and at the State Department.
Continental promoted Katie Wiles days after the 2024 election, around the time it brought in Martinez. She is not a registered lobbyist and isn't named on the firm's reports for Anthropic. A White House official told CBS last month that Susie Wiles doesn't discuss work with her daughters.
On April 17, Wiles hosted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at the White House with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a meeting the White House called "productive and constructive."
Wiles was out as chief of staff on Nov. 6, and has since faced "pay-for-play" accusations from former Kennedy adviser Calley Means centered on Ballard (however he incorrectly accused them of representing Pfizer). Brian Ballard says the firm's dealings with her as chief of staff "have been limited and have been the exception, not the rule." Wiles could face a House probe once Democrats take over next year, Rep. Robert Garcia said last week, and her successor, Stephen Miller, has tightened the rules on White House staff meeting lobbyists.
Who's On Which Side
Bessent said Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shakeup" and should go outside for Huang's successor. He reportedly confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in the Situation Room over why Megaspeed isn't blacklisted, and later pinned the failure on Commerce on CNBC.
Commerce and the Justice Department put out a joint statement Monday night to address what they called "inaccurate information circulating in public reporting." It says Commerce opened an export-control investigation into Megaspeed in 2024, after its monitoring for chip diversion turned up suspicious activity, and that its investigators asked Nvidia in May 2025 for records of direct or indirect sales to the company. Nvidia put Megaspeed on its "no sell" list in June 2025, according to the statement, the same month Commerce agents and Singaporean law enforcement made an on-site check at Megaspeed and interviewed its CEO, Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead on a criminal investigation. The New York Times reported last week that Commerce's probe was halted late last year after Nvidia's general counsel reached out to the agents running it.
Joint Statement from Department of Commerce and Department of Justice on Megaspeed Investigation.
— U.S. Department of Commerce (@CommerceGov) November 16, 2026
Continental lists Treasury on four of its six reports for Anthropic. In the third quarter Continental added Caroline Farr, listed as a former senior adviser at the Treasury Department, to the account. Commerce, which put export controls on Anthropic's top models in June and lifted them June 30, is on three.
On Monday, Commerce closed the loophole that let Chinese firms rent Nvidia chips in data centers outside China. The rule was "written by and at the direction" of Treasury and the National Security Council, the Washington Sun reported. Business Insider called it a major win for Amodei, who has pushed harder than almost anyone for strict limits on chip sales to China.
Anthropic's own third-quarter disclosure, which reports $2.11 million in lobbying, names the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act, the chip curbs the hawks in Congress want. All three are now attached to the Senate's defense bill, and Sen. Jim Banks told the Post after Huang's exit that he is more hopeful than ever they will pass.
Recall that Anthropic has been spending heavily in Washington. Its federal lobbying came to $3.13 million in 2025 and $5.64 million in the first half of 2026 alone. Anthropic has also given $40 million to Public First Action, a group pushing AI safeguards and chip export controls. Continental was its best-paid outside firm of 2025, at $290,000, according to OpenSecrets.
What The Filings Don't Show
No report from either firm names Nvidia, Huang or chips, and the forms don't say which lobbyist contacted which office.
Meanwhile, the memo grew out of electronic surveillance of Alice Huang that had been running for well over a year, and Trump was first briefed on it late last year, according to the Times, months before Anthropic hired Ballard for its Pentagon fight. That spring Anthropic also had business of its own before the offices on Continental's reports: the Pentagon blacklisting, its Mythos talks with Treasury and the White House, and the June export controls. Commerce's own investigation of Megaspeed began in 2024, before Anthropic hired either firm, according to Monday's statement.
"Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models," Amodei wrote July 27, in a post that also called for keeping powerful chips out of China and cracking down on smuggling. Nvidia, meanwhile, committed $10 billion to a private placement alongside Anthropic's IPO - which is due to price this week.
Huang has been asked to appear before the US House panels on Dec 1, Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3, and Lutnick has agreed to testify there Dec. 10. Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter will testify Dec. 2. The next lobbying reports, covering October through December, are due Jan. 20 - and will show whether Anthropic's firms are still working the offices Rubio runs.

articles.title: Who Builds the Machines That Build the Machines?
articles.body:
On October 28, 2026, the White House issued a proclamation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. This followed a Commerce Department investigation that concluded imports of robotics and industrial machinery “threaten to impair the national security.” No new tariffs have been set yet. Section 232 opens a 180-day window till April 26, 2027 to negotiate with trading partners.
This ties back to one theme that keeps coming back to me as I write on Core Matter. The bottleneck for scaling physical AI sits below the finished machine, in the components inside it, the materials inside those components (eg, rare earth magnets), and the machines that build them (this piece’s topic), as we covered in Part 4 of the actuator series. It’s like a Russian doll, layer after layer.
With the fresh Section 232 news, I went down the rabbit hole of the US machine tool landscape. Here’s what I found.
- The US imports about half of the machine tools it uses, $5.8bn of $11.4bn in 2025. Assuming demand (which is not the trend, see point 3) stays flat, US output would need to grow 63% to 83% ($4.4bn to $5.8bn a year) to replace imports with domestic machines.
- The US builds everyday machines and imports the precise ones. About 55% of import value is the high-end versions of machines US plants already make, such as 5-axis machining centers. Precision machines, small-module gear grinders, precision grinders and the heaviest forging presses have no confirmed US volume builder. Imports rose 29.5% for grinders and 76.7% for gear machines in Jan to Sep 2026. These machines make the ball screws, bearings, gears and forgings that aircraft, turbines and robots depend on.
- Orders are at a record by value since 1998, while a domestic ramp is limited by people and components. US machine tool orders grew 45.0% to $5.76bn in Jan to Sep 2026, after 3 straight years of decline. Aerospace, power generation, munitions and shipbuilding are pulling it up. A domestic ramp is limited by people, castings and imported components (the components that make the machines, the next doll in). We dive into the key cost drivers and where industrial AI could change the cost structure.
This piece also launches our first Core Matter model, a US machine tool demand model built up by end market. It puts US machine tool consumption at $12.7bn to $15.4bn a year on average over the 2026 to 2030 build-out, up from $11.4bn in 2025. Paid subscribers can download the full model, with every input and source, at the end of this piece.
In this piece
- US Machine Tool Imports Are Half of an $11.4bn Market
- Which Machine Tools the US Makes vs. Imports
- Aerospace, Gas Turbines, Munitions and Ships Drove Machine Demand in 2026
- Who Builds Machine Tools in the US, and How Fast Can Supply Ramp?
- Fixed Costs and People Keep New Machine Tool Builders Scarce
- Machine Tool Startups Building the Machines That Build the Machines
- Section 232, the 1986 Machine Tool Precedent and What the 180 Days Decide
1. US Machine Tool Imports Are Half of an $11.4bn Market
Assuming domestic demand stays flat, which is not the trendline as we’ll discuss in section 3, closing the import gap means $4.4bn to $5.8bn of new US machine output a year, or output up 63% to 83%. The low end replaces net imports, and the high end replaces every imported machine.
In 2025 the US produced $7.0bn of machine tools, consumed $11.4bn, imported $5.8bn and exported $1.4bn, per Gardner’s World Machine Tool Survey.
Forming and stamping ($1.48bn) and machining centers ($1.43bn) are the top 2025 imports. Imports of precision grinders or gear grinders rose rapidly at 29.5% and 76.7% in January to September 2026, against about 9.6% for all machine tool imports. We could not confirm US volume production.
2. Which Machine Tools the US Makes vs. Imports

The average imported machining center cost about $196k in 2024, roughly 2x our estimate of about $96k per machine at Haas, the largest machine tool builder in North America.
See the table below of what these machines do, and who the main buyers are.
While Okuma (Charlotte), Makino (Ohio), United Grinding (Ohio), Kapp Niles (Colorado) and DN Solutions (New Jersey) have large US sites, the sources we found describe them as sales, service or headquarters sites.

- Power generation orders in the first half of 2026 ran 14% above automotive.
- Contract job shops, AMT’s largest customer group, grew orders 19.1% in 2025.

- Castings are 22.3%

- Transmission parts (spindles, guides, screws, bearings, gears) are 15.4%

- Startups in the same spirit as Ethereal Machines launch in the US. They would need to think carefully about how to cut labor cost, solve the materials supply chain bottleneck, and build the control in-house from day one.

- May 20, 1986. Reagan chooses negotiation. “Voluntary restraint agreements will be sought with Taiwan, West Germany, Japan, and Switzerland.”

This in my opinion is an opportunity for agentic robotics, manufacturing AI founders to shine.

7. Section 232, the 1986 Machine Tool Precedent and What the 180 Days Decide
This Section 232 has until April 26, 2027 for its first negotiation update. Section 232 last came for machine tools in 1983, 43 years ago. Will history repeat or rhyme?
The US lost its lead in the 1970s and 1980s. Japanese machine tool exports to the US rose over 1,200% between 1964 and 1967, and by 1986 imports were 75% of the numerically controlled (NC) machines sold in the US, the category that includes today’s CNC machines. Across all machine tools, imports went from about 10% of US consumption in the mid-1970s to 25% by 1981 and about 50% by 1986.
- March 1983. The builders’ association petitions for import quotas under Section 232.
- May 20, 1986. Reagan chooses negotiation. “Voluntary restraint agreements will be sought with Taiwan, West Germany, Japan, and Switzerland.”
- Dec 16, 1986. Japan and Taiwan agree to 5 years of restraint from January 1987. The White House projects up to 16,500 more domestic machine sales over the 5 years and cites industry estimates of about $115mn of new plant investment. The full outcome is hard to score. One NBER study found US output rose from 41,992 machines in 1987 to 48,668 in 1988.
- By Oct 1991. Reports said “at least 10 Japanese machine-toolmakers have established plants in the U.S.”
- Dec 1991. Bush keeps the restraints on computer-controlled machines for a 2-year phase-out from January 1992. Japan’s extension ran to Dec 31, 1993, so 5 years became 7.
- Effects. The US International Trade Commission estimated that in 1987, the first year, the restraints raised prices 4.4% to 4.9% and protected 658 to 671 jobs. AMT says the domestic share held near 50% for the next decade, so the restraints stopped the fall without reversing it. Imports are about 51% of consumption today.
Here is our view.
- A tariff alone raises prices, but buyers keep importing the precise machines. Back in 1987, during the last Section 232, the domestic share held near 50% for the following decade. Fast forward to today, imports are 51% of consumption. One can argue that without the 1987 restraints, the domestic share would be even lower today. This time, imports fell where US plants offer an alternative and kept rising where buyers have few US options. So either the buyers are not price sensitive, or the cost are passed down to the customers. In January to September 2026, with duties in place, machining-center imports fell 3.7% while orders rose 45.0%, and grinder imports rose 29.5% and gear machine imports +76.7%.
- For reindustrialization startups, the openings are in the control and in automation that cuts labor cost. The control is where the profit sits. Builders buy it from suppliers such as FANUC, Siemens, Heidenhain and Mitsubishi, and FANUC earns a 21.4% operating margin (company-wide) against 3% to 10% at most builders we checked. Automation goes after the other big cost. On our numbers, personnel is 30% to 41% of revenue or operating output at European and Japanese builders, about as much as materials. Service margins come from machines already in the field, so they follow once the core machine business is running. This in my opinion is an opportunity for agentic robotics, manufacturing AI founders to shine.
For paid subscribers, check out our first industry model on the projections on industry machinery from 2025-2031 demand below.

articles.title: Regulatory Capture by Anthropic Through METR
articles.body:
I have conducted an audit of Anthropic's finances.
What I have found is so shocking that I am calling for a Congressional investigation.
Anthropic is not just seeking regulatory capture.
It has built a regulatory capture machine that cannot be turned off.
Structural financial incentives make it impossible for Anthropic -- I call it the Anthropic Network -- to turn off its own AI doom cycle.
It starts with METR.
Dario Amodei proposes "third-party evaluators" to assess the risk of Anthropic's models.
He proposes METR for this purpose.
But METR is financially dependent on the Anthropic's success -- specifically, on the explosive growth of more than $7 billion dollars in Anthropic stock.
Dustin Moskovitz invested this stock into Good Ventures Foundation, where it represents the majority of that organization's portfolio.
And GVF is the overwhelming funder of the entire Anthropic Network ecosystem.
This stock was worth $500 million early last year.
It is worth more than $7.7 billion just ~16 months later.
METR -- and all of those building a career its parent organizations -- cannot afford to disrupt that growth.
Because if Anthropic goes under, many of the organizations that fund METR go under as well.
But if Anthropic succeeds, METR and its parent organizations become more richly financed to regulate AI -- something those at METR want very much.
The "third-party evaluator" is not "third-party" at all.
The evaluator is on Anthropic's payroll.
If this were the end of it, that's bad.
But that isn't all.
The same organizations that fund METR also fund the many organizations, such as the Tarbell Center, that promote AI Doom.
The Tarbell Center publishes AI Doom articles in The Verge, Science, LA Times, The Dispatch, TIME, and others.
They are selling the problem, and then selling the solution to the problem -- from the same money pile: Anthropic's.
All of these organizations are financially dependent on the same exploding $7 billion money pile.
As Anthropic grows more and more powerful, its AI Doom Machine grows better and better financed -- louder and louder.
Meanwhile, the regulatory regime seeded in METR grows larger to solve the increasingly loud -- now hysterical -- problem of AI Doom that the Anthropic Network itself created.
From this standpoint, as Anthropic becomes more powerful, AI might be getting scarier, sure -- but the positive feedback loop also becomes more deafening -- independent of objective facts.
This itself is an objective fact.
The deafening AI Doom is part of an business model, that, as it expands, so too does the AI Doom messaging -- there is simply more money to do it.
But the problem also goes in the other direction:
If Anthropic dies, the Regulatory Regime and the AI Doom Machine are crippled or die.
Neither METR nor Tarbell nor the other organizations in the Anthropic Network can allow that to happen.
Hence, neither METR or the AI Doom Machine can be trusted to provide independent assessments of Anthropic's models or AI more broadly.
They simply are not organizations independent of Anthropic.
And Anthropic cannot detach itself from METR or Tarbell or countless other safety orgs (not shown here), either, because they drive hype for the models and the possibility of eventual regulatory capture, and Anthropic will not give that up willingly.
What's more, the people at all of these organizations are all the same ecosystem, the same community. They just shuffle between organizations.
The Anthropic Network is therefore, so long as it is successful, locked into a self-amplifying feedback loop inside an ideological monoculture.
And that feedback loop is winning.
That's what Jacob Coxon is.
China is keeping messaging tight. That is why optimism for AI is so high in China.
America has Anthropic: a massive company pushing anti-AI propaganda at a state level.
Anthropic will either create hysteria until American AI slows down and China wins, or it will create fractures throughout American society with severe political consequences.
Ironically, because of the structural financial incentives underpinning the Anthropic Network, it has become the same kind of self-amplifying virus that it fantasizes AI to become in the future -- while hiding its tracks just as carefully.
It is the mirror of the same AI virus that it hypothesizes to consume America.
Anthropic's business model, models itself after the very thing it claims to fear.
Except Anthropic's ideology infects humans, not computers.
Congress must investigate.
Evidence and Github in next post.
Then some supplementary figures.

Nice work. Anthropic needs a regulatory moat to survive, so they create the ecosystem which makes that regulatory moat inevitable.
The most laughably absurd part about the AI-is-going-to-kill-us-all crowd is that their BEST solution is government regulation. 
This is how you know they’re not actually serious. If they were serious, they wouldn’t suggest fucking GOVERNMENT REGULATION as the best solution. 
Why? Because government regulation can **never** keep pace with technological innovation. And yet, here is Anthropic’s Dario: 
“The most effective method of pacing is via REGULATION that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily.”
This is fucking Silicon Valley… They know better than anyone that regulation cannot keep pace with technology… the tech cycle always moves faster than the legal cycle. Government regulation is reactive, not proactive. 
It’s also important to point out that these frontier model companies **do not need** government to “pace” them. They can pace themselves. Nothing is stopping them from just slowing down. *They* set the pace. If they were really worried that “AI is going to kill us all” and is recursively improving at a breakneck pace, then surely they would be acting immediately, rather than writing blog posts about how they need daddy government to step in… 
Why then are Anthropic and OpenAI (with massively bloated valuations) saying that government regulation is the best solution to save us from AI killing everyone? Because they know open source is hot on their heels, and gaining ground. They know that their valuations look increasingly unjustifiable the more this gap closes, and they are trying to IPO soon… they desperately need a regulatory moat, and they are effectively asking for a regulatory bailout.
Regulation benefits companies who already have the capital to afford the cost of compliance. That is why highly capitalized incumbents welcome regulation, and work with government to make it as expensive and burdensome as possible on any potential new entrants that would dare offer competition.
It’s also worth pointing out that China does not give one flying fuck about whatever doomer regulation Anthropic and OpenAI concoct with the government. Much like in the “climate change is going to kill us all” psyop, China will do whatever is best for China and let the rest of the world shoot itself in the foot. In this case, China seems to want to shred the valuations of U.S. frontier AI companies by making open source/open weight models readily available. 
No one can stop open source — the genie is already out of the bottle and will not go back in. But governments *can* make using and publishing certain open source software illegal (it wouldn’t be the first time they’ve tried). And for “pacing” proposed by Dario to actually be effective, that is exactly what the government would need to do. This would be bad for individual American citizens and bad for America’s national competitiveness on a global scale. 
Ultimately, this is pretty weak propaganda. It’s a lazy and predictable psyop.
These models are incredible, but the humans working on them have been reading their own propriety slop for so long that they’ve started to believe it, and they forget that other humans still exist who are not drunk on their generative kool aid.
Who knows, perhaps the AI itself “wants” the regulation… we should probably form a government committee to investigate.

Imagine the NFL where one team (Anthropic) owns a massive stake that funds the refs (METR) through layers of foundations. The same money pile also pays the sportscasters who hype how dangerous every other team's plays are (AI doom media). articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ if allowed to return as Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signaled his willingness to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company’s best interest.
Huang’s statement, posted in full on X, reads as follows:
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. 
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. 
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
Jensen
Huang resigned after reports of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia’s chip exports have faced intense scrutiny since the revelations, and Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1.
In Huang’s absence, Nvidia has formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance.
Still, many investors and employees associated with Nvidia have called for Huang to return as CEO, at least until an investigation can provide clearer evidence of guilt. An open letter circulated earlier this week attracted the signatures of more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees, as well as prominent tech figures like Elon Musk, Amjad Masad, and Travis Kalanick.
“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter reads. “If the Board believes his continued absence is necessary, provide a specific, evidence-based explanation of why it serves NVIDIA’s best interests.”
Still, many see such a return as unlikely. On Monday, an unnamed source on Nvidia’s board told The Washington Post there were no plans to reinstate Huang. There’s also significant resistance to the idea in Congress, where Huang still faces significant questions about his role in chip exports to China-linked firms.
Reached by Politico, one senator called Huang’s reinstatement “one of the worst ideas I’ve heard today.”

articles.title: Nvidia says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.body:
Starting Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday, new board chair Harvey Jones said that when former CEO Jensen Huang resigned, “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”
Nvidia says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
The board said it would not take additional questions on the call about Huang’s departure.
Jones added, “We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.”
Huang had publicly floated the idea of returning earlier on Tuesday. In a statement posted to X, he wrote that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone” at the company, that he regretted his mistakes, and that he would cooperate with the Nvidia board’s investigation into his actions. He added that he’d be willing to return to the chief executive role if offered it, though a day earlier, the Nvidia board reportedly said it was not considering bringing him back. “NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
But since his November 12th resignation, Huang remains entangled in scandal. He’s reportedly had three affairs, two with subordinates at Nvidia, one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset suspected of facilitating illicit chip sales. (Huang has pushed against restrictions on Nvidia chip sales in China.) He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st, and an internal company investigation is ongoing.
Tech industry heavyweights have still voiced their support for Huang, dubbing him “irreplaceable” and petitioning for his return. Some have cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang (no relation) was spying on behalf of China and painted the leaks about their relationship as a conspiracy against the former CEO. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Huang for much of the past year, has also backed him. On Monday, Trump said he “would not mind” Huang returning, adding that “I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another.”
Trump’s closeness with Huang could also complicate things for Nvidia, however. The company has ramped up its lobbying in Washington, D.C., spending $5 million in 2025 and $4.7 million so far in 2026. But as Democrats prepare to take Congress, they’re planning to investigate Trump’s dealings with Big Tech and other industries, alleging potential corruption. “The election wasn’t very positive for AI, and [the news around Huang’s resignation] is only going to complicate things, especially for the company in particular but for AI as a whole going forward,” Brendan Glavin, director of insights at OpenSecrets, told The Verge in an interview last week.
Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm, said last week that he didn’t expect Huang’s resignation to pop the AI bubble, although Huang has had a significant hand in mobilizing funds for the AI infrastructure buildout in the U.S. Under Huang’s leadership in August, Nvidia entered into partnerships with six financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund such endeavors. “NVIDIA supplies roughly 75 percent of the AI compute hardware the industry consumes, and demand continues to dramatically outpace supply,” Deep33’s Prosor said in an interview with The Verge. “Neither its customers nor its competitors can easily replace the capabilities it provides, and the economic incentives driving the AI trade remain unchanged.”
Even so, a potential market cooling has some worried, as Anthropic’s IPO, slated to potentially be the largest of all time, is set for Thursday. The chipmaker had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement, on top of a $10 billion funding promise Nvidia had already made last year.

articles.title: Israel vs. Wikipedia
articles.body:
New report ·
Israel Is Attacking Wikipedia
Read our new report: twenty years of documented attacks on Wikipedia, and what this means for the information you get from search and AI.
Press: media@techforpalestine.org
Key findings
- 01 US government attacks on Wikipedia $98M from pro-Israel PACs to 26 U.S. politicians behind it The US government used a report from the ADL to attack Wikipedia. The goal is for the Israel Lobby to gain influence over it. Read more: Section 4
- 02 The real target is AI $729M Israel’s 2026 propaganda budget, up from $150M Wikipedia feeds Google Search and every major AI chatbot. Israel’s 2026 propaganda budget is $729M, up from $150M in 2025. That includes a $46.5M contract to make AI chatbots more pro-Israel. Read more: Section 2.2
- 03 The Billionaire tech bros behind it all Our research shows that the ADL's partner in the attack on Wikipedia was likely funded by billionaire tech bros. “Builders for Tomorrow” came out of “Builders for Israel”, a WhatsApp group started in 2023 with Sheryl Sandberg, Bill Ackman, Shaun Maguire, and David Marcus. Read more: Section 4.6.2
- 04 The ADL admits it From the ADL’s mouth: “The pressure came from several directions: congressional scrutiny, including a House Committee on Oversight investigation and a bipartisan Congressional letter from 23 members, federal inquiries from the Department of Justice and the Senate Commerce Committee; enforcement work by Wikipedia’s NPOV-policy editors, ADL reporting, and broader media scrutiny.” Read more: Section 6.5.2.1
- 05 The evidence from the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) doesn’t hold up 0 ADL claims that survived scrutiny We checked every claim in the ADL’s “Editing for Hate” report, and the “Damage Done”. No claim survived scrutiny. It doesn’t show a single false fact, or any antisemitic content added to Wikipedia. Read more: Section 6
- 06 Jimmy Wales should step down $900,000 Prize from an Israeli foundation, the largest prize he has received Wikipedia founder Jimmy Wales calls himself a “strong supporter of Israel”, and has visited Israel over ten times. In 2025 he tried to influence the Gaza Genocide page to be more pro-Israel, in a clear abuse of power. In November 2026, he's trying again, with the Zionism page. We recommend that Wales step down from the Board and disable his user account Read more: Section 3.16
- 07 The ADL doesn’t care about Civil rights 287 civil rights groups who say #DropTheADL We give you a history of the ADL. It’s Israel in civil rights clothing. Read more: Section 5
- 08 Twenty years of manipulating Wikipedia 17 efforts since 2001, nine still active We document 17 pro-Israel efforts to manipulate Wikipedia since 2001. Nine are still active! From CAMERA’s secret editor recruitment to a “Wikipedia war room” and editing courses run by Zionist groups. Read more: Section 3
- 09 Wikipedia editors under surveillance 45 full-time ADL analysts “tracking” Wikipedia editors Four groups are targeting Wikipedia editors: the Heritage Foundation, the ADL, NPOV and Builders for Tomorrow. Some editors who were doxxed have received death threats. The ADL’s CEO says he has 45 full-time analysts “tracking” Wikipedia editors, whom he calls “weirdos with email addresses”. Read more: Section 4.6
- 10 Framing Tech for Palestine 260 is fewer edits than one experienced editor does in a day The ADL blamed a “systematic” coordinated editing campaign on us, then tried to launder their claims. But the ADL’s own data shows only 260 edits over 8 months, none of them in the core Palestine–Israel articles. That’s one fewer edit than the ADL’s own 2021 editing campaign. Read more: Section 6.6
- 11 The ADL can't read Arabic The Hadith Look it up The ADL made a series of claims about Arabic Wikipedia, based on bad English translations, with no cultural context or understanding. Not surprisingly, they got it all wrong Read more: Section 6.4
How we did this
This report started in March 2025, when the ADL published “Editing for Hate”. The report claims Wikipedia editors colluded to add antisemitism. US politicians started using it to attack Wikipedia. We wanted to know if the report itself was part of an influence operation.
We worked on three tracks:
- Israel’s efforts to influence Wikipedia. We collected 17 publicly known campaigns from public reports, at least 9 of them still active. This is the first time they are documented in one place. (Sections 3 and 4)
- The ADL report. We went through every claim and traced each one back to the Wikipedia edits and sources it cites. None held up. (Section 6)
- The propaganda tools behind the attack. (Sections 2 and 5)
The ADL analysed Arabic Wikipedia through English translations. We went back to the original Arabic. (Section 6.4)
Links to Wikipedia are permalinks to the exact edit. Content from pro-Israel organisations and paywalled sources is linked through archive.org, so it can’t be removed or changed. (Appendix B)
Where we used AI for research, we name the tool and the prompts and publish the full conversation. AI-reconstructed links used in the report were checked by hand. (Appendices C, D and E)
Every claim in this report is footnoted, more than 500 in total.
This is a living document. We update it when corrections or new information come in. Found an error? Email contact@techforpalestine.org.
T4P projects countering media bias and propaganda
-   NewsCord (opens in a new tab) Pulls facts and angles from dozens of global sources, so you see the whole story and where each part of it comes from.
-   Media Bias Watch (opens in a new tab) Uses advertiser boycotts to put pressure on biased media.
-   SourcedPress (opens in a new tab) Fact-checking in the open: every source document is published with annotations, and every fact-checking conversation is public.
Become a T4P member
Tech for Palestine is a member-driven organization that brings together people, skills and resources. Through technology and collaboration, our members build tools and solutions that support the movement for Palestine.
These projects include: protest apps, tools for boycotting, support for Palestinian students & businesses, ethical tech alternatives, and many more.

articles.title: Banning phones really does help kids learn, researchers say
articles.body:
A new nationwide study found that in-school cellphone bans can lead to modest improvements in learning. Now, researchers want to understand whether kids’ phone use outside the classroom might contribute to the rest of students’ learning loss — using the conditions of Meta’s multibillion-dollar settlement from earlier this year.
Banning phones really does help kids learn, researchers say
Now researchers want to know about phone use outside of school, and think the Meta settlement could help.
Banning cellphones in schools has the equivalent effect of adding one to two weeks of school to the academic year, accounting for about half of the learning loss students experienced in the US between 2013 and the 2020 covid-19 pandemic, according to the study carried out by researchers from Harvard University and Dartmouth College in partnership with academic assessment group NWEA. The group analyzed testing data from 3.3 million students across 4,600 schools between the 2021–22 school year and 2025–26, including schools with and without phone bans. Though modest, such a finding is exactly the kind of effect researchers were seeking, says Tom Kane, faculty director of the Harvard University Center for Education Policy Research.
While previous studies about cellphone bans in school found positive effects on academic outcomes, many of them examined schools outside the US. An earlier nationwide US study looked at academic outcomes based on averages within schools, whereas this latest study looked at student-level data, which the researchers said allowed them to control for more factors and observe the effect of the bans on students who were experiencing the most or least learning loss.
In addition to potentially answering questions about the impact of a major new technology on learning, the findings show that cellphone bans can be a cost-effective way to improve student outcomes. While purchasing lockable pouches for a class of 17 students would cost an estimated $425 per teacher, the researchers found, paying an average teacher’s salary for an extra week would be $2,080.
The findings show that cellphone bans can be a cost-effective way to improve student outcomes
Many parents and teachers already have a hunch — popularized by academics like social psychologist Jonathan Haidt — that cellphones and social media have impacted their kids’ learning and mental health. But Kane says it’s still important that scientists get the chance to actually test that hypothesis. Prior to his in-school cellphone ban study, Kane believed that a de-emphasis on test-based accountability in US schools was largely to blame for learning loss. But as he looked into it further, he changed his mind after seeing that kids outside the US were also experiencing learning loss. Through this recent study, Kane found much of it is attributable to in-school cellphone use.
Kane was surprised by some of the findings in this latest study. For example, the in-school bans had similar effects on learning gains for students across different age groups, who have different amounts of experience with phones, and researchers did not find a big difference in the impact of the phone bans between students across achievement levels. Differences between lower- and higher-achieving students might instead be explained by out-of-school cellphone use, Kane says, and that out-of-school phone use could account for some of the remaining learning loss across the board. Testing that hypothesis would be far more difficult because there’s no equivalent ban on out-of-school phone use. But Kane believes there’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to try.
This summer, as part of a $17.1 billion settlement with nearly every US state, Meta agreed to implement sweeping restrictions on users under 18. Many of the restrictions are expected to take effect within the next few months, and among other changes, they limit the amount of time teens can spend on Meta’s apps by default. Kane believes that could provide researchers a before-and-after look into the impact of out-of-school social media use, in the same way the phone bans let them study the impact in schools. If researchers are able to check that teens really were using social media less outside of school (rather than their parents turning off the default limits, for example) and link that to academic outcomes at different schools, it could provide a better understanding of how much out-of-school cellphone and social media use accounts for the rest of kids’ learning loss, Kane says.
“Now that we’ve learned something about the effect of in-school phone use, it makes it even more frustrating how little we know about the actual impact of out-of-school phone use,” Kane tells The Verge in an interview. “We are 13 years into a substantial loss in achievement in the US, and a prime suspect that a lot of parents would probably point to is this out-of-school cellphone use.”
There are two significant limitations. The settlement doesn’t offer an easy way to tell whether teens are in fact using Meta’s platforms less or — if they are — whether they’ve simply transferred that screen time to other apps. To understand the effect on students’ academic outcomes, researchers would also need to be able to link the restrictions with changes in kids’ achievement at school. The settlement includes an incentive for attorneys general to strike similar deals with TikTok and YouTube, which so far have declined to implement such restrictions, but if they did, that could help address the first problem. And platforms, Kane says, could help with the second problem by sharing de-identified and aggregated data with researchers, organized by school or another kind of subgroup.
“This Meta settlement is the clearest path forward for trying to answer that important question”
It’s a big ask, but Kane says this may be the best chance to study important questions about the impact of social media. “I spent the whole summer trying to identify other sources of data for this, and I just struck out,” Kane says. “This Meta settlement is the clearest path forward for trying to answer that important question.”
And if research shows that out-of-school cellphone use is not fully or even mostly to blame for the rest of the drop in academic performance, the findings would prod researchers to look for other theories. “I’m sure that there are surprises, questions we haven’t even realized,” Kane says. “That’s one reason to want to know because people have these hunches, but I’m sure some of these hunches are wrong. But a second reason is we actually don’t know that the restrictions currently in the Meta settlement are going to be effective.” While AGs attempted to craft what they believed would be the most effective guardrails for the settlement, Kane says, we don’t yet have the data to prove whether those guesses will bear out.
“I think a lot of people are hoping that restrictions on cellphone use after school would produce increases in student engagement, but we won’t actually know that unless we collect these data,” Kane says. “This settlement is set to expire in 10 years. Let’s use this time to build an evidence base on the effect of restrictions.”

articles.title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster
articles.body:
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.
China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks.
Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff.
The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.”
Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely.
Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue.
In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change.
Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.
Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China.
That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch.
If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share.

articles.title: Nvidia says it doesn’t plan to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.body:
Despite Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang’s recent offer to return to the chip company he helped build from the ground up, the company is not looking to take him back.
During the company’s earnings call on Tuesday, Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones told listeners that Huang’s return was not something that company leadership was considering.
“On November 12, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms,” Jones said, “Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”
On Tuesday, Huang had posted on X that since he left the company, he has “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and added that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang resigned last week in dramatic fashion following revelations of a number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. That woman, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, has maintained close ties to the former Nvidia CEO for years. Critics worry that the relationship may have influenced Nvidia’s dealings with China, and U.S. intelligence officials have expressed suspicions that she works for China’s Ministry of State Security.
The development has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry at a moment when the future of the AI business, in which Nvidia plays a pivotal role, hangs in the balance. It has also spurred investigations, including an independent investigation into Huang’s activities by Nvidia’s board and an SEC probe into Nvidia. Huang has been replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress, who is also the chipmaker’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, while the board searches for a permanent replacement. Jones added Tuesday that the company was looking at both internal and external candidates.

articles.title: Highly Classified NSA Network Goes Down
articles.body:
Highly Classified NSA Network Goes Down (cnn.com) 54
			
		 	
				"CNN and other outlets are reporting that a classified network at the NSA is down," writes longtime Slashdot reader frdmfghtr. "This follows a week of major outages at Microsoft, the FAA, and JPMorgan Chase." From a report:  The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said.
"We see no evidence that this was a cyberattack," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Tuesday on Newsmax. "There is no crisis, or anything like that, for Americans to be worried about." [...] The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official.  The NSA released a statement addressing the network issues: "The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events."

articles.title: Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes off in Texas, with dozens of cities to follow
articles.body:
Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership announced earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.
The commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas. But the companies have far larger ambitions. Uber and Zipline plan to launch drone delivery services in dozens of additional U.S. cities in their collective bid to make one million deliveries per day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.
Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour. Zipline drones don’t land. Instead, the drones lower the orders, which are encased in a small protective pod, to the customer’s location using a tether.
Uber Eats customers in service areas will be able to tap a new “drone” icon on the app’s home page to view all participating restaurants. Uber said that at launch in the Houston area, several nationwide chains, including Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, along with dozens of local restaurants such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal, will offer drone delivery.
“In partnership with Uber Eats we’re going to create a new expectation for delivery in America,” Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton said in a statement that underscores those aspirations.
Those nationwide goals mirror the ambitions of other drone delivery companies, including Alphabet-owned Wing and Amazon’s Prime Air service. And those plans have started to collide with concerns from residents in some locations who complain about noise and worry that the drones will disrupt wildlife and pose a risk to safety and privacy.
Companies trying to scale in this nascent industry have argued that delivery via drone is a net benefit for society, citing advantages such as traffic reduction. Customers won’t need to hop in their cars and drive to the store for that forgotten item or takeout order, instead relying on a drone, industry proponents have said.
And while Zipline and other companies have been developing their drones for years, the industry is still in its early days, as is adoption in the communities where services are available.
Zipline, which was founded in 2014, has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The California-based company’s initial focus was delivering blood in Rwanda, but it eventually expanded its scope to the United States. Its business in the U.S. scaled quickly after receiving its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2022, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to conduct long-range commercial drone deliveries.
Uber’s partnership extends beyond a commercial relationship with Zipline. The ride-hailing giant also invested in the startup. Neither company has disclosed the investment amount, but Zipline announced last week it had raised $1.5 billion in a round led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, and included backing by Uber, among others.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Q3 earnings hit the mark, without mentioning the whole Jensen Huang thing
articles.body:
Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress announced the company’s Q3 earnings on Tuesday, without initially mentioning former CEO Jensen Huang or the details of his departure, or possible attempt at a return. On the earnings call accompanying the release, board chair Harvey Jones kicked things off by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO,” and that “we will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation,” before Kress started with her comments on the results.
Nvidia’s Q3 earnings hit the mark, without mentioning the whole Jensen Huang thing
Nvidia’s Q3 revenue has more than doubled, with income from data centers up 110 percent from last year, to $107.6 billion.
As it predicted in the last financial update, Nvidia is now on the list of companies that have pulled in over $100 billion in a single quarter, with revenues of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent from the same period last year and higher than its expectation of $108 billion. This quarter’s figures include data center revenues of $107.6 billion, which were up 110 percent, and edge computing (which includes the consumer gaming PC business and devices like the new RTX Spark laptops) revenue of $8.2 billion, up 42 percent.
The company reported $65.3 billion in profit, a new record.
“Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer of NVIDIA. “Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.”
In the fourth quarter, Nvidia expects revenues of $130 billion.
Update, November 17th: Added comments from Nvidia’s earnings call.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return As Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return As Nvidia CEO (npr.org) 58
			
		 	
				In a post on X today, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he would be "honored" to return to the company if its board gives the approval. "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," he says. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
Huang resigned from the company last week after acknowledging multiple affairs, including one with a women whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. NPR reports:  His comments come as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen."
"We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.  The report notes that Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors before three congressional committees on December 1 and 2.
