articles.title: Cerebras Disaggregated Inference
articles.body:
We’ve deployed Cerebras Wafer Scale Engines with GPUs to deliver lightning-fast tokens at scale
The world is hungry for ultrafast tokens. In 2026, Cerebras saw an insatiable demand for fast inference, both on our inference cloud and via our partners. To meet demand, we began developing disaggregated inference: GPUs handle prompt processing (prefill) and Cerebras systems handle output generation (decode).
This solution is now in production and delivers five times more tokens per megawatt at the same ultrafast Cerebras speeds.
We can now serve more ultrafast tokens via Cerebras Inference Cloud to meet market demand. Infrastructure partners can also leverage the Cerebras disaggregated solution to achieve more ultrafast tokens in their own datacenters.
Alongside our recently announced CS-4, our dramatically scaled manufacturing, and our planned 700MW of data center capacity, disaggregated inference will enable Cerebras and partners to serve many more ultrafast tokens in 2027 and beyond.
In this blog we cover:
- The need for more ultrafast inference capacity
- Why Cerebras is advantaged for decode
- Cerebras disaggregated inference production results
- Cerebras disaggregated inference for infrastructure partners
The need for more fast inference capacity
Agentic applications like Muse, Copilot, and Codex are scaling rapidly and require highly interactive inference to keep users engaged. To meet the growing demand of these applications in a power-constrained environment, our industry must deliver significantly more inference capacity per megawatt, at response speeds that make these applications useful.
Sources: Goldman Sachs Research, “AI Agents Forecast to Boost Tech Cash Flow as Usage Soars,” May 20, 2026; Goldman Sachs data center capacity estimates, as reported by Investing.com, November 6, 2026.
That is why Cerebras invested in disaggregation. Pairing a prefill accelerator for prompt processing with the Cerebras System for response generation increases token throughput per megawatt while preserving Cerebras’ ultrafast generation speeds. For inference providers, that means more capacity to serve customers and greater revenue potential from the same power budget.
Why Cerebras is advantaged for decode
An inference request has two main stages. Prompt processing, known as prefill, processes the input and produces intermediate model state. Response generation, known as decode, uses that state to generate output tokens. There are many ways to split the inference workload, including draft–target and attention–FFN among others, but separating prefill from decode is uniquely advantageous when the goal is highly interactive inference.
Decode is autoregressive. That means the model generates one token at a time, using each generated token as an input to generate the next. Each step means reading model data from memory again, so memory bandwidth matters a lot. In the ultrafast inference domain, SRAM-centric chips have an advantage because they can keep that data on-chip and read it much more quickly. Cerebras takes this to wafer scale, with tens of gigabytes of SRAM and tens of petabytes per second of memory bandwidth on a single chip—350× the SRAM capacity and 5,400× the memory bandwidth of a typical GB300 GPU. This allows the Cerebras System to fit more concurrent requests and model layers directly on the chip, enabling the CS-3, CS-4, and CS-5 to achieve ultrafast speeds at an attractive throughput.
Cerebras disaggregated inference production results
Pairing Cerebras systems, which are optimized for ultrafast decode, with accelerators well-suited to the compute needs of prefill, such as AMD Instinct GPUs, allows the delivery of an immense amount of ultrafast inference at scale. In a production deployment on the Cerebras Inference Cloud, AMD Instinct GPUs process prompts, and Cerebras CS-3 systems generate responses. Moving prompt processing to GPUs allows Cerebras systems to devote their serving capacity to response generation. In our measured production deployment, this combination delivered 5X the throughput per megawatt of a CS-3-only configuration, with no loss in token generation speed.
Source: November 14th shared GPT-OSS-120B endpoint via the Cerebras Inference Cloud throughput per megawatt before and after enabling disaggregated inference, normalized to the aggregated inference baseline (1×).
We plan to deploy disaggregated inference broadly across hundreds of megawatts in the Cerebras Inference Cloud and in partner deployments by the end of 2027. Our aim is to increase the ultrafast inference capacity available for our customers.
Cerebras disaggregated inference for infrastructure partners
The Cerebras disaggregated inference solution was also built for our partners to adopt. Infrastructure partners can deploy disaggregated inference clusters based on Cerebras-provided reference architecture, co-locating their chosen prefill accelerators and Cerebras systems within a unified network. For software integration, partners can either integrate with the Cerebras end-to-end disaggregated software stack or a decode-only SDK.
The end-to-end disaggregated software stack is best suited for partners optimizing time-to-market. It consists of:
- A disaggregated inference framework to route requests between prefill and decode pools and manage replica capacity and health.
- A prefill engine to process prompts using open-source inference engines like vLLM or SGLang.
- A Cerebras decode engine for response generation on Cerebras systems.
- KV Portal software, an interface to transfer intermediate model state, including key-value caches, between prefill and decode engines over RDMA.
The decode-only SDK is best suited for partners optimizing for control. With the decode-only SDK, partners can bring their own inference framework and prefill engine to the Cerebras decode engine and KV Portal software. In addition, the decode-only SDK provides development aids such as a mock Cerebras decode replica and a reference integration to an open-source disaggregated inference framework and prefill engine.
Early-access partners, including Amazon Web Services, Fireworks AI, Gimlet Labs, and General Compute, already have access to the Cerebras disaggregation solution for their deployments. We are now expanding access to additional partners looking to bring ultrafast inference to their customers at scale.
To discuss the results, solutions, or deployment opportunities in more detail, contact us here.

articles.title: The DOJ says it’s investigating Megaspeed
articles.body:
The Justice and Commerce Departments said that they are investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center company intertwined with the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after reporting suggested an investigation had been halted last year.
The DOJ says it’s investigating Megaspeed
The announcement comes a week after revelations that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang was romantically linked to a leader at Megaspeed.
“While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting,” the departments said in a statement issued Monday evening. The departments acknowledged there’s been “significant public attention” on Megaspeed.
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week after reports he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, who Megaspeed says left the company in August 2025. The scandal has raised questions about national security, and sparked scrutiny of Nvidia’s handling of exports of its chips to China and Megaspeed’s possible role in moving along Nvidia’s chips.
Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed “came to a sudden halt” late last year after its investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel, claiming Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler gave Nvidia permission to reach out. The case was then “quickly” handed over to the DOJ, according to the Times.
The announcement today says the DOJ took the “lead role” in the investigation last year:
After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The statement doesn’t go into detail about the current status of the case, but it says the DOJ and Commerce Department “will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

articles.title: Nvidia Rejects Jensen Huang's Offer to Return as CEO
articles.body:
Nvidia Rejects Jensen Huang's Offer to Return as CEO (apnews.com) 30
			
		 	
				Nvidia's board has unanimously rejected former CEO Jensen Huang's offer to return, despite public support from President Trump and prominent Silicon Valley figures. The decision came as Nvidia reported blockbuster third-quarter revenue of $116 billion, double the year-earlier figure. The Associated Press reports:  The embattled company's board of directors "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of Nvidia's quarterly earnings call before yielding to Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who is running the company as a permanent replacement is sought. [...] Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said in a social media post that if the board decided that his return was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and the country, he would be "honored to answer these calls." He acknowledged making "serious mistakes" in his personal life.
The turmoil notwithstanding, Nvidia blew past Wall Street expectations for the third quarter, pulling in $116 billion in revenue, double the level from a year ago. The company also posted net income of $2.70 per share, beating estimates of $2.48 per share. Nvidia stock shot up 5.2% in after-hours trading. Referring to Huang's replacement, Jones said, "We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person."   Nvidia also announced a new board committee overseeing national security and trade compliance amid investigations into alleged AI chip smuggling to China.
Further reading: Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion

articles.title: Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion
articles.body:
Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion (ft.com) 15
			
		 	
				Nvidia stopped separately disclosing its Singapore sales (source paywalled; alternative source) after changing its geographic revenue reporting methodology from customer billing addresses to headquarters locations, obscuring a business that generated $104 billion in external revenue in 2025, up 72% from the previous year. The Financial Times reports that the change has drawn scrutiny amid U.S. investigations into whether Singapore-based Megaspeed helped smuggle Nvidia chips into China. From the report:  "There is now a lot more focus on Nvidia's Singapore business and questions about who its end customers are," said an investor who is investigating Nvidia's dealings in south-east Asia. The Singapore accounts show that the subsidiary booked $117.8 billion of revenue in the 12 months to January 2026, including $13.6 billion of sales to another Nvidia company. Given the nature of the Singapore operation as a global hub, customers it serves are from all over the world. Only a small quantity of the chips Nvidia sells ends up in or goes through Singapore. The Singapore subsidiary generated just $53 million of profit in the year to January 2026, suggesting limited scope for Nvidia to benefit from Singapore's low corporate tax rates.
[...] Singapore's outsized role as a revenue generator for Nvidia used to show up in the company's overall results. In January 2025, the US company reported that Singapore was its second-biggest geographic area by revenue, based on customer billing location. The Singapore office generated $23.7 billion of revenue, behind only the US and representing 18 per cent of global income, based on customers' billing location. The annual accounts said that most of the business was generated by customers using the Singapore office to centralize invoicing and that most of the products were shipped elsewhere, with less than 2 per cent of revenue tied to chips that landed in the city-state.
As recently as July last year, Nvidia reported that the Singapore office accounted for 22 per cent of total revenue. This was around the time Nvidia said it began cutting ties with Megaspeed, following US Department of Commerce investigations into the business. Nvidia then changed its financial reporting methodology and stopped splitting out revenue that went to the Singapore office. Before the 2025 reporting change, Nvidia said in its financial filing that it booked sales based on the billing locations of its customers, but that the end customer's location "may be different than our customer's billing location." It added that "most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant," according to the filings.

articles.title: You can now preorder the Flipper One that puts a Linux computer in your pocket
articles.body:
After first announcing its Flipper One last May, which the company describes as an “open Linux multi-tool built for high-performance computing and IP networking,” Flipper Devices has launched a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign where you can preorder the device for $399 with shipping expected to start in July 2027.
You can now preorder the Flipper One that puts a Linux computer in your pocket
The Flipper One is launching for $399 and is expected to ship to Kickstarter backers next year.
The Flipper One is more expensive than the company’s popular but controversial Flipper Zero wireless hacking multitool, which is currently available for $169. However, Flipper Devices points out that the new Flipper One isn’t a successor to the Flipper Zero, but a completely different product.
While the Zero’s capabilities focused on NFC, RFID, infrared, and Sub-1GHz wireless frequencies, the much larger Flipper One offers expanded connectivity with two gigabit ethernet ports, PCIe, SATA, and USB 3.0 interfaces, and Wi-Fi 6e support. There’s also an M.2 slot for connecting modules that include a 5G modem and a mesh networking LoRa radio that can turn the Flipper One into a walkie-talkie.
It’s still pocket-friendly, but the Flipper One is powered by an 8-core RK3576 ARM processor with a dedicated NPU and a GPU that supports connectivity to an external display over USB-C or HDMI. Flipper Devices suggests the One can be used as everything from a networking diagnostics tool to a media player when connected to a TV. It runs Flipper OS, which is based on Debian Linux and features an open source firmware so that users can develop their own apps, tools, and uses for the device.

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he’s open to returning in first statement since resignation
articles.body:
In his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO last week, Jensen Huang struck a contrite tone, saying that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence contact.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in the written statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
Huang said he had seen support from investors and employees and was willing to come back as CEO to help the company navigate "complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in the statement.
Sources told CNBC Monday that the board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO.
Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO, putting together an online petition with more than 180,000 signatures.
President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia.
Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang, Nvidia's founder, admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had a liason with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence. Jensen Huang also reportedly had romances with employees at Nvidia.
Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. Its board of directors said on Friday that it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role.
Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.
Here is the entire statement from Huang:
Over the past week, I've been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life's work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation.
Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
Correction: Jensen Huang is the former CEO of Nvidia. His title was misstated in a headline on an earlier version of this article.

articles.title: US Officially a Measles Endemic Country
articles.body:
US Officially a Measles Endemic Country 2
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years.
Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has previously said losing elimination status won't lead to changes in the federal response.
"We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities," Schwartz said on Tuesday. "Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks."

articles.title: A US Federal Women's Prison Became a "Rape Club"
articles.body:
Reporting Highlights
- A Cascade of Cases: We found more than 185 cases of officers accused of sexually abusing people in women’s prisons over the past five years, sometimes beating them or denying them food or medical care.
- Broken Promises: Officials vowed to reform the system in 2021, but more than a dozen current and former federal prison employees said they had seen few or no meaningful improvements.
- “A Hunting Ground”: Though some abusers have been prosecuted or removed, insiders say the culture of impunity that allows officers to prey on women remains.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
Officer Felix Wilder sauntered around the women’s prison like he owned the place.
Prone to showing up to work in gold chains and stylish jeans instead of his concrete gray government uniform, the slender 35-year-old moved, one woman said, “like he had just gotten off of a horse from a long ride.” He spoke slowly and eyed the prisoners as they walked through the drab buildings and shadeless yards of the secluded federal lockup in Aliceville, Alabama.
By the fall of 2024, some of the women there had begun to notice him hovering over a soft-spoken immigrant from Mexico who’d been in prison for only a few years. Ela, as she asked to be called, had dark hair, dark eyes and children to get home to back in Utah. Wilder was just a little too close, a little too familiar.
Ela’s cellmate, who asked to be identified as Ana, watched it all with unease. At 40, she knew exactly what that kind of attention from an officer could mean in a women’s prison.
For 15 years, Ana had served her time at Federal Correctional Institution Dublin, a low-security prison in California, where officers had preyed on the women in their care. Sexual misconduct became so rampant that staff and prisoners alike called it a “rape club.” Eventually, the FBI intervened, and prosecutors charged the warden, the chaplain and nine other officers with sexually abusing female prisoners. Hundreds of women — including Ana — came forward to tell what happened to them, not just to investigators, but also to outside lawyers who sued the system to demand change at the Bay Area prison.
Ana had hoped to leave that all behind when she was transferred out of Dublin. But tucked between the pine trees and low-slung churches of rural Alabama, the Aliceville prison had its own brand of menace. The facility had newer buildings but fewer freedoms. The roofs leaked, and sometimes the air smelled faintly of mold. The shorthanded staff often locked the women in their cells for days at a time.
And then there were officers like Wilder, who seemed to be choosing their targets.
Thousands of miles from families they couldn’t call during yet another lockdown, Ana and Ela became allies. They paced. They picked at the lukewarm meals delivered on Styrofoam trays. They stared out the narrow slit of a window.
And then Ela broke down, sobbing as her words tumbled out into the stale prison air.
Two years earlier, an officer had pulled her into a closet and raped her, she told Ana, her voice quavering. Now, she said, it was happening all over again — but this time it was the stylish officer in jeans: Felix Wilder.
Ela said she’d reported the first assault and nothing happened. Now, she didn’t know what to do. If the prison didn’t care about one rape, why would it care about two?
As she listened, Ana felt a dull rage churning in her stomach. She thought of all the things she’d seen and survived at Dublin: the rapes, the harassment, the uncertainty of a life subject to the whims of lascivious men with badges. As she tried to comfort her sobbing cellmate, she wondered whether Aliceville was any better. Maybe, she thought, no place was.
Sitting on her metal bunk, she opened the little address book she’d bought from the prison commissary and flipped to the phone numbers for the lead attorneys in the class action lawsuit against Dublin. “Here,” she told Ela, “you can talk to them.”
The arrests and subsequent convictions of Dublin staff — 10 in all — marked the largest sex abuse scandal in the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ history and a rare moment of accountability in a troubled system where many women had learned to stop expecting it. Suddenly, every branch of government stepped in. A federal judge appointed an outside monitor. A slew of agencies issued reports, and the Justice Department dispatched attorneys to visit and evaluate women’s facilities. Congress passed a law to create a new, independent office to oversee the prison system.
But after the judge made that unprecedented move to appoint outside oversight, in early 2024 the bureau abruptly announced it would shut down Dublin and transfer its more than 600 women — including Ana — to lockups across the country.
Then, quietly, the window of accountability shut. Little appeared to have come of the promised reforms, the site visits and the reports, and Congress never appropriated funding for the new oversight office. More than a dozen current and former federal prison employees told ProPublica and The Marshall Project they’d seen few or no meaningful improvements. One Justice Department official said the only obvious sign of progress was new sexual assault prevention posters.
“Nothing has really changed,” said Alix McLearen, a top Bureau of Prisons official who retired in 2024 after serving as the agency’s first administrator overseeing the women and special populations branch. “We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.”
An official with the federal prison workers union who — like nearly every current employee interviewed for this story — asked not to be named for fear of retaliation, put it even more bluntly: “Nothing has been done to effectively change sexual abuse of inmates within the BOP. Not on a large scale or small scale.”
For the last five years, the culture that spawned a rape club at Dublin has persisted across the system. Reporters at ProPublica and The Marshall Project set out to determine how pervasive the problem of staff sexual abuse inside federal women’s prisons is — and what, if anything, officials have done to solve it. What we found was sexual assault, misconduct or harassment at most of the 27 facilities that currently hold women. We identified more than 185 cases in which prison employees have been accused of sexually abusing people in women’s prisons since 2021, the year the Dublin scandal broke. The cases implicate more than 96 officers at 16 prisons. Of those, just 19 officers have been arrested or convicted.
In some cases, officers withheld food or medical care, or threatened to put women in solitary confinement if they refused to comply with sexual demands, court records allege. In others, officers locked them in windowless closets or bathrooms, choked them, or forced them to use sex toys or have sex with each other. In more than a dozen instances, the assaults were so brutal that the women were left bruised and bleeding.
Though some abusers have been prosecuted or removed, insiders say the culture of impunity that allows officers to prey on women remains. Officials have repeatedly refused to acknowledge or failed to act on signs of sexual abuse, we found. More than 25 women said that they were abused by officers who had been reported or investigated before, according to lawsuits we reviewed. In some cases, officers have covered for their abusive colleagues, court records allege. Other times, staff say that they, like the prisoners, have hesitated to report misconduct for fear of retaliation.
At a prison camp in West Virginia, an officer who’d been investigated repeatedly for suspected abuse — but allowed to remain on the job — raped a woman so forcefully that he tore her vaginal lining, according to a lawsuit she filed last year. The officer has been charged with sexually assaulting her and two other women at the camp and has pleaded not guilty. His case is set for trial early next year.
At Federal Medical Center Carswell, a facility in North Texas, an officer allegedly forced two women to have a threesome with him in his office, where he’d rigged up a doorbell to alert him if anyone came by, court filings show. A civil lawsuit has been stayed pending a criminal investigation.
And at Aliceville, Wilder, the officer who allegedly assaulted Ela, also abused at least 17 other women, many of whom were facing deportation after they finished serving their sentences, according to court records and interviews. He allegedly didn’t stop until the FBI showed up at the facility in the fall of 2024, and federal prosecutors eventually charged him with sexually abusing seven women. He has pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial.
“I’m pretty sure everybody knew what was going on and they just didn’t care,” one of the women told ProPublica and The Marshall Project in a phone interview from the federal prison in Fort Worth, Texas.
We found that abuse continued even as the facilities kept passing federally mandated sexual assault prevention audits. The Texas medical facility had a flawless audit the same year the FBI arrived to investigate a paramedic whom at least 18 women have accused of sexual assault, records show. Likewise, Aliceville got perfect marks during the same time period that Wilder was allegedly preying on Ela and other women.
The officers union called sexual abuse “completely unacceptable” and blamed persistent staffing shortages for helping to create an environment that allows it to go undetected. “If we are serious about protecting inmates and maintaining safe, secure federal prisons, we have to address the staffing crisis head-on,” the union said in a statement, noting that more watchful eyes would mean “fewer opportunities for inappropriate conduct to occur behind closed doors.”
Bureau of Prisons spokesperson Randilee Giamusso said the federal prison system has “zero tolerance” for sexual abuse and harassment. “We take all allegations of sexual abuse seriously,” she said.
Giamusso highlighted the bureau’s recently revamped policy on sexually abusive behavior, which is intended to ensure that allegations are more thoroughly investigated. It also eliminates any mention of transgender or intersex people, whom federal law identifies as particularly vulnerable to sexual abuse in prison. She did not provide further details or address any specific cases, saying the bureau does not comment on pending litigation. Officers mentioned in this story, as well as representatives for the prisons, either did not respond or declined to comment on specific allegations.
As Ana and the other Dublin women, now scattered to other facilities, realized that no one was going to stop the abuse, they began to take matters into their own hands. Across the country, they encouraged other women to speak out about what had happened to them — and told them what they could do about it.
The volume of abuse allegations ballooned so rapidly that the legal team handling the Dublin case had to refer scores of potential clients to other lawyers, some of whom have taken on so many federal prison sex abuse cases that it’s become the primary focus of their law practice. We continued receiving new lawsuits, tort claims and allegations of abuse up until publication of this story.
“There has been so much reporting on Dublin as an aberration,” said Susan Beaty, one of the lawyers spearheading the class action suit. “But I think it’s actually incredibly representative. I think it’s happening at basically every BOP women’s prison.”
As she comforted her cellmate at Aliceville, Ana thought back to her first months at Dublin — before she’d learned how to recognize abuse in prison and before she’d seen just how much of it there was.
Back then, around 2010, it seemed that almost every day she saw a handful of women eating Mexican takeout for lunch — hot meals too mouth-watering to have come from the spartan prison kitchen.
At the time, Ana was just 25 and at the beginning of a lengthy sentence stemming from her involvement in her husband’s drug-trafficking operation. So while she suspected the smuggled-in meals were the sign of some nefarious quid pro quo arrangement with the officers, she didn’t ask questions, partly because she was afraid and partly because the women shared their coveted contraband meals. “So I would just eat it and shut up,” she said.
Under federal law, all sexual contact between prison staff and people in custody is a felony — and for good reason. Prisoners cannot meaningfully give consent when they’re propositioned by people who control every aspect of their lives, from when they get fed to whether they face disciplinary sanctions that could land them in solitary confinement. So although prison sex abuse sometimes involves violent rape, it often relies on subtle coercion and grooming.
Poor conditions and scarcity behind bars turn basic necessities into valuable commodities that officers can leverage to create the illusion of a “relationship” — one built on exchanging sexual favors for extra privileges and little gifts, like contraband makeup, extra tampons or a few more minutes at visitation.
As one high-ranking prison official explained: “The women are getting small trinkets. It’s not big things that we can trace. He’s bringing in a hamburger, a Subway sandwich. It’s heartbreaking to look at the value of the things that are being passed.”
Many times, those seeming relationships turn volatile — and violent. In Ana’s case, it began when one Dublin officer started being unusually nice to her, according to her lawsuit. He’d rush across the unit to unlock doors for her or call her into his office to talk alone. Ana thought they’d developed a rapport. But over time, he groomed her with personal questions and meager privileges. Once, he told her he’d had a sexual dream about her. Then, according to her lawsuit, he kissed her and eventually raped her.
Telling prison investigators didn’t seem like an option; Ana had already learned the hard way about the risks of reporting errant staff. A few years earlier, she had helped another prisoner file a complaint about staff misconduct. Afterward, she said, both women were sent to solitary confinement. For two weeks, Ana spent 23 hours a day locked in a cell barely bigger than an elevator. She got cold food, had no access to the phone and was barred from seeing visitors.
Prison officials often isolate those who report abuse, ostensibly for their own protection, even though the Justice Department has found this practice has a “chilling effect” that discourages people from reporting abuse. A federal prison spokesperson said the agency’s policy does not require that people who report abuse be put in solitary — but that sometimes it is the only adequate option.
It’s not just prisoners who are afraid to report wrongdoing. Although staff are required to report misconduct under bureau policy, in lawsuits and interviews, officers say they, too, worry about retaliation.
“You see all the sexual abuse, how they treat inmates. If you bring that to their attention, it’s like you’re doing the wrong thing,” said a former correctional officer at the prison camp for women in Bryan, Texas. In 2024, she reported several co-workers for having sexual contact with incarcerated women. She resigned last year after the warden moved to fire her for unprofessional conduct, documents show.
Even when witnesses or victims do report abuse, investigators rarely conclude that it occurred. As of 2022, less than 10% of allegations against Bureau of Prisons employees were substantiated, meaning investigators found it more likely than not that the abuse happened in those cases. In some instances, investigators decided there was evidence the abuse didn’t occur. But more than 75% of the time, they said there wasn’t enough evidence to make a determination either way.
Officers accused of abuse face an internal disciplinary process that can take years. In many cases, they can simply retire or resign, knowing that the agency will no longer have jurisdiction to punish them once they leave. They could still face criminal charges — but bureau insiders say that many cases don’t reach that point because investigators abandon the criminal probes when an officer resigns. “Staff would know that if they were having sex with inmates, the worst that would happen is that you would have to find a new job,” one former prison official said.
The landmark law intended to combat sex abuse, the 2003 Prison Rape Elimination Act — widely known as PREA — mandates employee training and regular audits but lacks a serious enforcement mechanism. Auditors are primarily looking for policy compliance, not signs of abuse. “A facility may have widespread sexual abuse, but they’re still meeting compliance on the things they’re required to do,” said Kendra Prisk, a PREA auditor who has evaluated several federal prisons, including Aliceville.
